children.text: First-year university physics has a reputation for brutality, and students arriving from a good Physics 12 grade are often the most blindsided by it. They knew this material. That is precisely the problem.

It is the same physics with the training wheels off. In Grade 12 you were handed formulas and asked to use them. Here the formulas are derived, and the derivation is the exam — because the formulas you memorised are special cases, and this course spends its time outside the special case.
If a strong high-school student is suddenly underwater, that is not a talent problem and it is the most common story we see. Our
university physics tutoring
starts by fixing the assumption underneath, rather than drilling more problems.
Your kinematics equations were a special case
This is the single most valuable thing to understand in the first month, so it is worth doing properly.

You memorised five equations. Nobody told you they come with a condition attached, printed in small type at the top of the chapter: constant acceleration. Not sometimes. Always. That condition is the only reason they exist.
Watch what happens when it fails. Suppose
— acceleration that grows with time, which is what any realistic force gives you. Start from rest at the origin. How far have you gone at
Reach for the old equation and pick an acceleration. Use the value at t = 2, which is 12:
Wrong. Try being cleverer and use the average acceleration over the interval, which is 6:

Still wrong. The true answer is 8 m, and no choice of a single acceleration value will produce it, because the equation is not slightly off — it is answering a different question. It describes motion that never happened.
The actual method
Acceleration is the derivative of velocity, and velocity is the derivative of position. So go the other way — integrate:
At
m. That is the answer, and it is the only route to it.

Now look back at your five equations with this in mind. They are not laws. They are what you get when you integrate a constant acceleration once, and then again — the integration already done for you, and handed over with the condition quietly dropped. That is why they break: not because physics changed, but because you were only ever given the easy case.
Which is why the graph matters
Here is the same idea as a picture, and it is the one to keep.
Displacement is the area under the velocity-time graph. That is true always, for every motion, with no conditions on it whatsoever.

When velocity is a straight line — constant acceleration — the area is a triangle, and ½ × base × height is exactly the formula you memorised. The old equation was never a law; it was the area of a triangle. But when velocity curves, the triangle overshoots: 12 m where the truth is 8 m. Same picture, different shape, and only integration handles both.

This is also why calculus is a co-requisite rather than a nice extra, and why students who treat it as a separate subject struggle here. If the calculus itself is shaky, that is worth fixing first — we wrote about
what to review before a first calculus midterm
Energy, and the other formula that has a condition
The same trap, one chapter later. You learned:
Also conditional. It requires the force to be constant, and most interesting forces are not.
Compress a spring with stiffness
N/m by 10 cm. At full compression the force is
N. So the work is 20 × 0.1 = 2 J?

No. At the start the force was zero — the spring pushes back harder the more you squash it. The force ramped from 0 N to 20 N, and multiplying by the final value assumes it was 20 N the whole way. Integrate instead:

Exactly half the naive answer, because the force rose linearly and its average was 10 N rather than 20 N. Every "½" in the energy chapter — ½kx², ½mv² — is the fingerprint of an integral you did not do by hand.

So the pattern across the whole course: a formula from school, a hidden condition, and a university problem built specifically to violate it. Once you are looking for it, the course becomes far more predictable.
F = ma is a differential equation
This is the reframe that makes the rest of the course coherent, and it is rarely said out loud in a lecture.
You read
as an equation to solve for one of three numbers. It is not. Acceleration is
, so what Newton actually wrote is:

That is a differential equation — a statement about how velocity changes, not what it is. Whenever the force is constant, integrating it twice hands back your school formulas, which is why they worked. The moment the force depends on where you are, or how fast you are going, they stop, and the differential equation is all you have.
Falling, with air
Drop something and include air resistance, which grows with speed. Then the force on the way down is not constant — gravity pulls, drag pushes back harder the faster you go:
Watch what this predicts without solving anything. At the start
, so there is no drag and the acceleration is a full
m/s². As speed builds, drag grows, and the acceleration shrinks. Eventually drag exactly cancels gravity, the acceleration reaches zero, and the speed stops changing:
For an 80 kg skydiver with
kg/s, that is 60 m/s — about 217 km/h, and it is why a parachute is survivable rather than merely slower.

Notice what just happened. The acceleration went from 9.8 to 0 during the fall, so there is no single value to put into a kinematics equation — not the initial one, not the final one, not the average. The entire toolkit from Grade 12 has nothing to say about the most ordinary event imaginable: something falling through air.

And you got the most useful number — terminal velocity — without solving the equation at all, just by asking what happens when the acceleration stops. That habit of interrogating an equation before solving it is most of what separates a physicist from a calculator, and it is what the harder exam questions are testing.
Vectors get taken seriously
In Grade 12 vectors mostly meant "remember the minus sign". Here they are the language.
Components are not optional. Nearly every problem starts by resolving along sensible axes, and choosing bad axes turns three lines of algebra into a page.

The dot and cross products arrive with physical meaning rather than as arithmetic. Work is a dot product — it asks how much of the force points along the motion, which is why a force perpendicular to motion does no work at all. Circular motion is the cleanest example: the centre-pointing force does no work, so speed is constant while velocity changes constantly.
Torque is a cross product, and the direction is not a convention to memorise but the axis the thing turns about.
Where the marks actually go
Using a school formula outside its condition. This is the big one, and it produces a confident, tidy, wrong answer — the worst kind, because nothing feels off.
Starting with algebra instead of a diagram. First-year problems are longer, so a wrong setup costs a whole page rather than a line.

Substituting numbers too early. Do the algebra symbolically and the units check themselves, terms cancel, and you can see whether the answer is sensible. Substitute at line one and you are pushing decimals around blind.
Not checking limits. Set a variable to zero or infinity and ask whether the answer still makes sense. It catches errors instantly and it is what a physicist actually does.
How to study it
Derive the formulas once, by hand, rather than collecting them. The exam asks you to do it again in an unfamiliar case, and there is no way to fake that.
For every equation you use, be able to say what breaks it. If you cannot name the condition, you do not own the equation.
Do problems without numbers. Get to the symbolic answer, then substitute last.
Treat the calculus as part of the physics. dx/dt is not notation to survive — it is what velocity means.
Getting help with first-year physics

The students who struggle here are rarely struggling with physics. They are applying Grade 12 methods to problems designed to defeat them, working hard, and getting nowhere — which is demoralising in a specific way, because effort is not the missing ingredient. Our
one-on-one university physics help
works from your actual problem sets and past midterms.
Sessions run in person in Burnaby or online across Metro Vancouver, and online suits this material well — the working stays on screen and you can re-read the derivation afterwards.
Book a free 30-minute consultation

children.text: Calculus and
linear algebra

are two of the most important mathematics courses for university science, engineering and commerce. They're different in flavour — one about change, the other about structure — but together they form the backbone of quantitative study.

What You'll Learn Here

The key is to build genuine understanding — the intuition behind the methods — rather than memorising procedures.

At

Who Needs a Math Tutor in Grades 8–12?
A student in grades 8–12 benefits from a math tutor if they:
Consistently score below 75% on tests despite studying
Understand concepts in class but freeze during tests
Are entering Foundations of Math 10, Pre-Calculus 11/12 or Calculus and want a head start
Are enrolled in IB Math (AA or AI) or AP Calculus and need exam-specific preparation
Want to raise their grade to meet university admission requirements (UBC, SFU, BCIT, etc.)
Learn better with individual pacing rather than a 30-student classroom
If two or more of these apply, one-on-one
math tutoring in Burnaby
or Vancouver is one of the highest-leverage academic investments a family can make.
Why Grades 8–12 Math Is Different and Why It's Where Students Fall Behind
Elementary and middle school math is mostly arithmetic and pattern recognition. High school math is abstract, cumulative and exam-driven. Each course builds directly on the last:
Math 8/9 → Foundations of Math 10 → Pre-Calculus 11 → Pre-Calculus 12 → Calculus 12 / AP Calculus / IB Math

A weak foundation in one course doesn't just affect that year's grade — it compounds. A student who never fully understood factoring in Math 9 will struggle with rational expressions in Pre-Calc 11 which then undermines limits and derivatives in Calculus 12.
This is why generic tutoring or last-minute test prep rarely works long-term. Effective math tutoring in Vancouver and Burnaby needs to diagnose
where
the gap started, not just

Grade-by-Grade Breakdown: What Each Course Demands
Math 8 and Math 9: Building the Foundation

These years introduce integers, exponents, linear relations, polynomials and the first real exposure to algebraic thinking. Students who coast through Math 8–9 with shortcuts (calculator-dependence, memorized steps without understanding "why") often hit a wall the moment Foundations of Math 10 introduces more abstract reasoning.
What a tutor focuses on:
number sense, algebraic manipulation fluency and converting word problems into equations — the skill that underpins everything afterward.
Foundations of Math 10: The First Major Fork in the Road

Foundations of Math 10 (and its companion, Pre-Calculus 10 content) is where students decide their math trajectory for the rest of high school. Topics include systems of linear equations, factoring trinomials, surface area/volume, trigonometry of right triangles and function notation.

This course is frequently underestimated because it sounds "basic," but it's actually the course where a surprising number of B and C students quietly fall behind before Pre-Calculus 11. A Foundations of Math 10 tutor in Burnaby typically works on:
Solidifying factoring and algebraic fluency
Linking graphical and algebraic representations of functions
Word-problem translation (distance, rate, mixture, and finance problems)
Building exam-writing speed and accuracy under time pressure
Pre-Calculus 11: Where Algebra Gets Serious

Pre-Calculus 11 is widely regarded as the most conceptually demanding jump in BC's math sequence. Quadratic functions, radical and rational expressions, absolute value, and the introduction of the unit circle and trigonometric ratios all appear here — often within the same semester.
Students who don't have a Pre-Calculus 11 tutor in Burnaby or Vancouver often describe this course as "the year math stopped making sense." A skilled tutor breaks the course into its building blocks:
Quadratic equations: factoring, completing the square and the quadratic formula and
when
to use each
Rational expressions and equations (a leading cause of marks lost on exams)
Trigonometric ratios and the law of sines/cosines
Function transformations and graphing fluency
Pre-Calculus 12: The University Gatekeeper Course

Pre-Calculus 12 is often the single most important math grade for university admission in BC — many programs at UBC, SFU and BCIT explicitly require it. It covers transformations of functions, exponential and logarithmic functions, polynomial functions, trigonometric identities and sequences and series.
A Pre-Calculus 12 tutor in Vancouver typically prioritizes:
Logarithm and exponential rules (a frequent source of provincial-style exam errors)
Trig identities and equation-solving strategies
Function composition, inverses, and transformations
Strategic exam preparation for cumulative final assessments
Calculus 12: The Bridge to University Math

Calculus 12 introduces limits, derivatives and an introduction to integral concepts that are entirely new in structure compared to anything students have seen before. This is also where many strong algebra students struggle for the first time, simply because calculus
thinks
differently than algebra does.
A
calculus tutor in Vancouver
focuses on building conceptual intuition (what a derivative actually represents) alongside the mechanical skills (chain rule, product rule, optimization problems) needed to perform well on tests.
IB Math and AP Calculus: A Different Level of Rigor
Vancouver and Burnaby have a high concentration of IB World Schools and AP-offering secondary schools and both programs demand significantly more depth than the standard BC curriculum.
IB Math (Analysis & Approaches / Applications & Interpretation)

IB Math is assessed through both exams and Internal Assessments (IAs) meaning students need strong written mathematical communication, not just correct answers. An IB Math tutor in Vancouver or IB Math tutor in Burnaby typically helps students with:
Structuring and defending an Internal Assessment (a major source of stress for IB students)
Mastering the command terms IB examiners look for ("justify," "hence," "show that")
Paper 1 (non-calculator) and Paper 2 (calculator) exam strategy
Topic-specific support across both AA and AI pathways, including calculus, statistics and vectors
AP Calculus (AB/BC)

AP Calculus is a college-level course compressed into a high school timeline, assessed by a single high-stakes exam each May. An AP Calculus tutor in Burnaby or AP Calculus tutor in Vancouver typically works on:
Free-response question (FRQ) strategy, since these are scored very differently from multiple choice
Building exam stamina for the multi-hour AP exam format
Bridging AB and BC content gaps, especially for students aiming for a 4 or 5
Connecting AP Calculus performance to university credit and advanced placement opportunities
What Makes One-on-One Math Tutoring More Effective Than Group Classes?

Classroom teachers in Vancouver and Burnaby typically manage 25–35 students per math class. Even excellent teachers can't fully personalize pacing, explanation style or practice problems for every individual learner.
One-on-one math tutoring in Burnaby and Vancouver solves this in several concrete ways:
Diagnostic accuracy
— A tutor can quickly identify
which specific concept
(not just "which unit") is causing errors, whether that's sign errors in factoring or misreading function notation.
Pacing control
— Some students need to slow down on foundational algebra before tackling trigonometry; others are ready to accelerate. Group classes can't offer this flexibility.
Real-time feedback
— Mistakes are corrected the moment they happen, before they become ingrained habits that show up on test day.
Exam-specific coaching
— Provincial assessments, IB exams, and AP exams each have distinct formats and command-word expectations that benefit from targeted practice.
Confidence building
— Many students who "hate math" simply never had the chance to ask questions without judgment in a 30-person classroom.
How to Choose the Right Math Tutor in Vancouver or Burnaby
When evaluating a math tutoring program in Vancouver or Burnaby, look for these signals:
Curriculum alignment
: Does the tutor understand the current BC curriculum, IB syllabus, or AP Calculus framework specifically — not just generic high school math?
Diagnostic approach
: Do they assess where a student's understanding actually breaks down, rather than starting from the current textbook chapter?
Course-specific experience
: A tutor who has specifically taught Pre-Calculus 11, Pre-Calculus 12, IB Math, or AP Calculus will understand the exact exam patterns and common pitfalls of that course.
Communication with parents
: Regular updates on progress, not just a report card surprise in June.
Flexible, individualized sessions
: Group tutoring services can fall into the same one-size-fits-all trap as classrooms; true one-on-one instruction avoids this.
Build Math Confidence That Lasts Through Grade 12 and Beyond

Whether your child needs help with the basics in Foundations of Math 10, is preparing for Pre-Calculus 11 or 12, or is tackling the rigor of IB Math or AP Calculus, the goal is the same: real understanding, not just a passing grade.

children.text: After enough years of marking Pre-Calculus 12, you stop seeing individual mistakes and start seeing the same ten, over and over, in different costumes.

They are not careless errors, and telling a student to "be more careful" does nothing about them — because carelessness is not what is happening. Each one is a rule that is true somewhere else, applied where it does not hold. The student is not being sloppy. They are being consistent with a rule that was never real.
Here they are, with the counterexample that kills each. If you recognise your own work in several of these, that is normal and it is fixable — it is what
Pre-Calculus 12 tutoring
spends most of its time on.
1. The big one: (a+b)² is not a² + b²
This single mistake costs more marks in Pre-Calculus 12 than any other, and it survives all the way into university.
Test it. Let
and
Not close. Off by 24. And that 24 is not random — it is exactly 2ab = 2(3)(4). Here is where it lives:

Once you have seen the square, the mistake becomes hard to make. You are not forgetting a term from a formula sheet; you are claiming two rectangles of the picture do not exist. And notice when the wrong version accidentally works: only when 2ab = 0, which means a or b is zero. That is why it occasionally "checks out" and the habit survives.
2. The family it belongs to

The (a+b)² error is not one mistake. It is one instance of the deepest misconception in high-school mathematics: the belief that operations distribute across addition. Squaring does not. Neither do most things.
Square roots
With 3 and 4:
, not 7. If square roots did split across a sum, the 3-4-5 triangle would be a 3-4-7 triangle, and Pythagoras would never have got anywhere.
Logarithms
With a = b = 10:
, but
. The rule students are half-remembering is real, but it is about products, not sums:

That is the actual law, and it checks: log(100) = 2. Logarithms turn multiplication into addition — that is their entire purpose, and it is why they were invented. They do nothing for addition, and this confusion accounts for most lost marks in the logarithms unit.
Reciprocals
With 2 and 3:
, against

So the rule worth carrying is a negative one: unless you can name the law that permits it, do not move an operation through a plus sign. Multiplication distributes over addition. Almost nothing else does.
3. Dividing by a variable, and quietly deleting a solution
Solve x² = x. The tempting move is to divide both sides by x:
One answer. But x = 0 also works — 0² = 0 — and it has just been thrown away, because dividing by x assumed x ≠ 0 without saying so. Factor instead:

Both survive. The rule: never divide by something that might be zero. Move everything to one side and factor. This costs half a mark in Pre-Calculus 12 and entire questions later, because the root you delete is often the interesting one.
4. Squaring, and quietly inventing one
The mirror image. Solve √(x+2) = x. Squaring both sides:
So x = 2 or x = −1. But check them in the original, which is the step everyone skips. x = 2:

So the answer is x = 2 alone. The −1 is extraneous — squaring created it, because squaring destroys sign information: both 1 and −1 square to 1. Any time you square both sides, you have possibly manufactured a solution, and checking is not optional tidiness. It is part of the method.
Notice the symmetry with the previous one. Dividing loses roots; squaring invents them. Both happen because an operation that is not reversible was applied as though it were.
5. The inequality sign that should have flipped
Divide by −2 and the sign must turn: x < −3. Test it. x = −4 gives −2(−4) = 8 > 6 ✓. x = −2 gives 4 > 6 ✗. So the solutions really are below −3.

Students know this rule and still miss it, because they apply it when they see a negative sign rather than when they multiply or divide by a negative. Those are different triggers. And it gets far worse with variables: you cannot multiply an inequality by x at all without knowing x's sign, which is why rational inequalities want a sign chart, not algebra.
6. Answers that were never allowed
Solve and you get x = 2 for something involving
. But log of a negative number does not exist, and log 0 does not either — so the domain here is x > 3, and 2 was never a candidate. It has to be discarded regardless of how clean the algebra was.

Domains are not a formality at the start of the chapter. They are a filter on the answer at the end. Logs need positive arguments, even roots need non-negative ones, denominators cannot vanish — and a solution that violates any of these is not a solution, however tidy the working that produced it.
7. Notation that means something else
means
. It does not mean
. At x = 2 radians the first is 0.827 and the second is −0.757 — not merely different values, different signs.

It is an unfortunate notation and everyone trips on it once. The reason it matters is that the Pythagorean identity is written this way, and it is the most-used identity in the course. If you want that unit properly, we wrote a full guide to
trigonometric identities and equations
8. The transformation that goes the wrong way
shifts the graph three units to the
. Almost everyone's instinct says left, because there is a minus sign, and the instinct is wrong.
Do not memorise it — derive it in five seconds. Take
, whose vertex sits at x = 0. Now
. Where is g's vertex? Wherever the bracket becomes zero, which is x = 3. So the feature that was at 0 is now at 3: it moved right.

The reason is worth having, because it generalises to every transformation in the unit. The bracket does not describe where the graph goes. It describes what x has to be for the function to receive its old input. To feed f a 0, you now have to supply x = 3 — so everything happens 3 later, which is to say further right.

Get this backwards and you lose the transformations unit wholesale, since every question builds on it. Get the reason and you never need the rule: horizontal changes are always opposite to what they look like, and vertical ones are always exactly what they look like, because vertical changes happen outside the function where nothing is being undone.
Why these cost so much more than they look like they should
Read that list and each item seems minor — half a mark here, a sign there. But that badly understates the damage, for a reason worth understanding.

None of these are topics. They are sub-steps. Expanding a bracket is not a Pre-Calculus 12 question; it is a line inside a question about transformations, or logarithms, or rational functions. So an error in it does not cost you the mark for expanding brackets — it costs the question. A student who owns every idea in the course but expands (a+b)² wrongly will still lose marks across every unit, and their report will say they are struggling with Pre-Calculus 12 when they are actually struggling with Grade 9 algebra, at speed, under time pressure.

This is also why the marks are stubborn. More practice on the current unit does not help, because the current unit is not the problem. That mismatch — working harder on the wrong thing and seeing nothing move — is what makes students conclude they are bad at maths.
It also does not stop at Grade 12. Every one of these reappears in first-year calculus within about three weeks, where the pace is roughly double. We wrote about that in our guide to
limits and derivatives
— the students who struggle there are almost never struggling with calculus.
What actually fixes them
Test the rule on numbers. Every mistake above dies to one substitution. If you are unsure whether a step is legal, try a = 3 and b = 4 and see. Ten seconds, complete certainty.
Check your answers in the original equation, not the rearranged one. Extraneous roots are invisible anywhere else.
Write the domain before you solve, not after.
Learn one picture per rule. The square above is worth more than the formula it encodes, because you cannot misremember a picture the way you can misremember a line of symbols.
Look at your own past tests. The ten mistakes above are common, but you personally probably make two or three of them, repeatedly. Finding which two is worth more than any amount of general revision.
Getting help with Pre-Calculus 12

If marks are dropping and nobody can say why, it is very often one of these rather than the topic on the page. That is genuinely good news: a foundation error is a quick fix once it has been found, and finding it is what we do in the first session. Our
one-on-one Pre-Calculus 12 help

Sessions run in person in Burnaby or online across Metro Vancouver, aligned to the BC curriculum.
Book a free 30-minute consultation
and bring a recent test — the marked one, mistakes and all. That is the useful one.

children.text: "He understands it when we go through it, but then he gets them wrong on the test." Almost every parent who contacts a tutor says some version of this, and it is the single most useful sentence to unpack — because it describes two completely different problems that need opposite treatments.

Get the diagnosis wrong and months disappear. A student with a concept gap given more practice questions simply practises the misunderstanding until it is permanent. A student with a practice gap given more explanation sits through lessons they already understand, gets bored, and still runs out of time in the exam.
The distinction is not subtle once you know what to look for, and you can test it at the kitchen table in about ten minutes.
The two failure modes
A concept gap

The student does not understand what the mathematics means. They may still get answers right — by mimicking a worked example closely enough — which is exactly what makes this hard to spot from a report card.
It looks like:
They can do a question that matches an example, but stall completely when the wording changes
They cannot say why a step is done, only that it comes next
Wrong answers are wrong in strange ways — not close, but structurally off
They ask "what do I do here?" rather than "did I do this right?"
Progress collapses whenever a topic builds on the shaky one
A practice gap
The student understands the material. The knowledge is simply not fast or automatic enough to survive a timed test.
It looks like:
They can explain the method correctly, out loud, without notes
Mistakes are arithmetic slips, dropped signs, copying errors — "silly mistakes"
They run out of time, or rush the last questions
Homework is fine; tests are not
Shown the mistake, they immediately see it — no explanation needed
The ten-minute test
Here is the diagnostic, and it works because it separates knowing from doing.
Take a question they got wrong. Do not ask them to solve it. Ask them to explain how they would solve it — out loud, without writing anything and without touching the numbers.
If they can talk you through the method confidently and only fall apart when executing it — that is a practice gap.
If the explanation is vague, circular, or reaches for the textbook — that is a concept gap, regardless of what their homework marks look like.

The reason this works: explaining requires understanding, while doing can be faked by pattern-matching. Most school assessment rewards doing, so a concept gap can stay hidden for a long time — often until the course builds on it and everything appears to collapse at once.

A second, blunter version: ask "why does that step work?" A practice-gap student answers, sometimes impatiently. A concept-gap student explains what the step is again, more slowly. Watch for that substitution — it is the tell.
Why they need opposite treatments
A concept gap needs rebuilding, not repetition

More questions will not help, and can actively harm. Every repetition of a misunderstood method makes it more automatic and harder to dislodge. The fix is to go back — often further back than feels reasonable — find the idea that never landed, and rebuild from there.

This feels like losing ground. Parents often resist it, because the student is behind and going backwards seems like the opposite of catching up. But a concept gap is load-bearing: everything stacked on it is unstable, and time spent stacking higher is time wasted.
A practice gap needs volume and timing

Explanation is not the constraint — the student already understands. What they need is enough repetition that the method becomes automatic, and enough timed practice that exam conditions stop being a separate skill.

Re-teaching a practice-gap student is a common and expensive mistake. They already know it. What they cannot yet do is retrieve it in ninety seconds with a clock running, and no amount of further explanation builds that.
The same wrong answer, two different causes
Here is the whole problem in one line of a student's homework. They write:
It is wrong. The real expansion carries a middle term:
Now — and this is the point of this entire article — that identical mark on the page can mean two completely different things, and the paper cannot tell you which.
If it is a concept gap

The student believes squaring distributes across a sum. They are not being careless; they are applying a rule they think is real. So they will make this error every single time, calmly, and with no sense that anything is wrong. Their confidence is intact, which is exactly what makes it dangerous — nothing signals to them that they need help.
Ask them to check it and they cannot, because to them there is nothing to check.
If it is a practice gap

The student knows perfectly well that there is a middle term. Under time pressure, on question 14 of 20, they wrote the fast thing instead of the true thing. Ask them to look again and they will say "oh — 6x" before you finish the sentence.
Same error on paper. Opposite problems. Opposite treatments.
How to tell, in thirty seconds
Hand them a number. Ask them to try
in both sides.

A practice-gap student sees 16 against 10 and instantly knows what they did. A concept-gap student sees 16 against 10 and is confused — the numbers disagree and they do not know why, because their rule said they should match. That confusion is the diagnosis. It is not a bad sign; it is the most useful thing that could happen, because it is the first moment the gap has ever been visible.
One last detail, and it explains why this survives for years undetected. Try x = 0:

They agree. The wrong rule gives the right answer, because the term it omits is 6x, and 6 times 0 is 0. Every so often a student's broken rule produces a correct answer by accident, it gets a tick, and the rule is quietly reinforced. This is how a concept gap survives a whole term of homework that looked fine.
The trap: "silly mistakes"
This phrase hides both problems, which is why it is worth interrogating.
Sometimes a silly mistake really is one: a dropped minus sign, a misread digit. That is a practice gap, and repetition fixes it.

But often "silly mistake" is what a student calls an error they cannot explain. If they consistently make the same silly mistake in the same place, it is not carelessness — it is a misunderstanding wearing a friendlier name. The test is whether they can tell you why it was wrong. If they can only tell you that it was wrong, look closer.
Both at once

The honest complication: it is often both. A concept gap in one topic, and a practice gap everywhere else. The order matters — fix the concept first, then build the speed, because drilling an idea that is not yet understood cements the wrong version.

It also changes over a term. A student who started with a concept gap and has had it repaired will look, for a few weeks, exactly like a student with a practice gap — because that is now what they are. The diagnosis is not permanent, and it is worth re-running.
What this means for choosing help
It is worth knowing which problem you are buying help for, because they look identical from the outside and cost the same.
A homework club or worksheet service is practice. Useful for a practice gap; nearly useless for a concept gap
A group class re-explains the curriculum. Useful if the explanation is the constraint; not if the student needs volume
One-on-one tutoring can do either — but only if the tutor diagnoses first rather than starting from page one
This is the reason our
free 30-minute consultation
is a conversation rather than a lesson: the diagnosis genuinely determines what we would do, and getting it wrong wastes your money as well as your child's term.
What to do this week
Take one wrong answer from a recent test — not a homework question.
Ask them to explain the method out loud, without writing or touching the numbers.
Listen for whether they explain WHY, or only re-describe WHAT.
If they can explain it: practice gap. Give them volume and a timer.
If they cannot: concept gap. Stop the practice, go back, and rebuild.

That is a real diagnosis, and it costs ten minutes. It is worth considerably more than another purchased workbook — because the workbook is only the right treatment for one of the two problems, and you now know which.
If you would like a second opinion
We do this diagnosis at the start of every relationship, because starting to teach before you know which problem you are solving is guesswork. Our
one-on-one math tutoring in Burnaby
and science support work the same way, whether the answer turns out to be a concept gap, a practice gap, or the usual mix of both.
Sessions run in person in Burnaby or online across Metro Vancouver.
Book a free 30-minute consultation
— we will work through a recent test together and tell you honestly which of the two you are dealing with, even if the answer is that no tutoring is needed yet.

children.text: There are five gas laws in Chemistry 11, and that is four more than there needs to be.

Boyle's law, Charles's law, Gay-Lussac's law, Avogadro's law, the combined law — students dutifully memorise all five, mix them up under exam pressure, and pick the wrong one. But they are not five laws. They are one law, looked at from five angles, and once you see that, there is nothing left to mix up.
This guide covers the gas side of Chemistry 11 and the point where it meets stoichiometry. If the mole ratios themselves are the shaky part, start with our
step-by-step guide to stoichiometry
first and come back — this builds directly on it.
Kelvin is not a unit conversion
Before anything else, because it invalidates everything downstream if you get it wrong.
Gas law temperatures are always in Kelvin. Always. Not sometimes, not when the question says so — always. And the reason is not convention, it is arithmetic.
The gas laws contain ratios like

. A ratio only means something if zero on the scale means zero of the thing. Kelvin has that property: 0 K is genuinely no thermal energy. Celsius does not — 0°C is just a Tuesday in Vancouver. So the ratio 100°C / 25°C is not 4. It is meaningless.
Here is what it costs. Heat 500 mL of gas from 25°C to 100°C and ask for the new volume.
Done properly: 298.15 K → 373.15 K, and the volume goes to 626 mL.
Done in Celsius: 25 → 100 looks like a factor of four, giving 2000 mL.

That is not a rounding error. It is off by more than a factor of three, and it is the single most common way to lose full marks on a question you actually understood. Convert to Kelvin as the very first line of working, before you even decide which law you need.
Boyle's law, and why the graph curves
Squeeze a gas into half the space and the pressure doubles. Pressure and volume are inversely related, at fixed temperature and amount:
So 2.0 L at 1.5 atm, compressed to 3.0 atm, becomes
L. Double the pressure, halve the volume.
But the part worth actually understanding is the graph — because exams ask about it, and because it explains what "inversely proportional" really means.
Both panels show identical data. The left curves; the right is straight. Nothing changed except what we plotted along the bottom.
That is the whole point of the 1/V axis.
is a curve, and eyeballing a curve tells you very little. But rewrite it as
and it is just

— a straight line through the origin whose slope is the constant itself. A straight line is something you can draw with a ruler, measure, and extrapolate. This is why lab write-ups ask for P against 1/V rather than P against V, and "why is the second graph linear?" is a question that appears every single year.
Charles's law, and the rest of the family
Heat a gas at constant pressure and it expands. Volume and temperature are directly proportional:

Gay-Lussac's law says the same for pressure and temperature at fixed volume — which is why an aerosol can carries a warning about heat, and why a car's tyre pressure reads higher after a motorway run. Avogadro's law says equal volumes of any gas at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of particles, regardless of what the gas is.

Notice the shape of all of them. Each holds two things constant and relates the other two. They are not independent discoveries you must memorise separately — they are what is left of a bigger equation once you nail two variables down.
The one law they all came from
Here is the equation the whole family collapses into:
Pressure times volume equals moles times the gas constant times temperature. With
L·atm/(mol·K) when pressure is in atmospheres and volume in litres — and matching R to your units is worth one careful look before you start.

Now watch the five laws fall out of it. Hold n and T constant, and the right side is a constant, so PV is a constant — that is Boyle. Hold n and P constant, and V/T is constant — that is Charles. Hold n and V constant, and P/T is constant — that is Gay-Lussac. Hold P and T constant, and V/n is constant — that is Avogadro.

So there is one thing to remember, not five. And when a question changes conditions on a fixed sample of gas, you do not need to identify which named law applies at all — just cancel whatever does not change:

Take 2.0 L at 1.0 atm and 273 K, then double both the pressure and the temperature. The pressure would halve the volume; the temperature would double it. They cancel exactly, and the volume comes back to 2.0 L. That is a two-line answer with the combined law and a maze of substitutions without it.
Where the two halves meet
This is the reason the two topics share a unit, and it is the idea that makes both of them worth having.
Stoichiometry counts particles. Gas laws let you count particles without counting them — by measuring pressure, volume and temperature instead. Rearranged, the ideal gas law is a particle counter:

You cannot weigh a gas conveniently. But you can measure the volume it fills, the pressure it pushes with, and how warm it is — and that gets you the number of moles, which drops straight into a mole ratio.
Worked example
Zinc reacts with hydrochloric acid to give hydrogen gas. What volume of hydrogen comes from 5.00 g of zinc at 25°C and 1.00 atm?
Balance first — always. Zinc 1 and 1, hydrogen 2 and 2, chlorine 2 and 2. It balances.
Grams to moles:
mol.
Mole ratio: the balanced equation says one zinc gives one hydrogen molecule, so n(H₂) = 0.0765 mol as well.
Now the gas law does the last step. Convert 25°C to 298.15 K, then:
And sanity-check it: less than a tenth of a mole, so it must be well under 22.4 L. It is. That check takes three seconds and catches an entire class of arithmetic slips.
22.4 L/mol, and when you are allowed to use it
One mole of any ideal gas at STP occupies 22.4 L. It falls straight out of the ideal gas law with n = 1, T = 273.15 K and P = 1 atm:

It is a genuine shortcut and it saves real time. But it is only true at STP, and students reach for it constantly at 25°C, where it is simply wrong. If the question does not say STP, use PV = nRT and do the work. The shortcut is a special case, not a fact about gases.
Dalton's law, and the water you forgot about
One more, and it is the one that turns a textbook answer into a laboratory answer.
In a mixture of gases, each gas pushes with its own pressure as though the others were not there, and the total is simply the sum:

Which sounds abstract until you actually run the zinc experiment. Hydrogen is collected by bubbling it up into an inverted tube of water — and the gas you collect is not pure hydrogen. It is hydrogen plus water vapour, because the water is quietly evaporating into it the whole time.
At 25°C water vapour contributes 23.8 mmHg, which is 0.0313 atm. So if the total in the tube reads 1.00 atm, the hydrogen itself is only responsible for:

Redo the zinc calculation with 0.969 atm instead of 1.00 and the volume comes out at 1.93 L rather than 1.87 L — about 3% larger. Small, but it is the difference between a right answer and a nearly-right one, and "collected over water" is the phrase in the question that tells you it applies. Miss those three words and you lose the mark without ever knowing why.
Three to try
1. Boyle
A weather balloon holds 4.0 L at 1.0 atm at ground level. It rises until the pressure is 0.50 atm. Ignoring temperature, what is the volume?
L — halve the pressure, double the volume.
2. Charles, with the trap
1.50 L at 20.0°C is cooled to −10.0°C. Convert first: 293.15 K and 263.15 K. Then
L. Cooling shrinks it, so an answer above 1.50 L means a flipped ratio. And note the minus sign never appears in the working once you are in Kelvin — which is the point.
3. Gas stoichiometry
Heating limestone drives off carbon dioxide:
. What volume of CO₂ comes from 10.0 g of CaCO₃ at STP?
M(CaCO₃) = 40.08 + 12.01 + 3(16.00) = 100.09 g/mol, so n = 0.0999 mol. The ratio is 1:1. At STP you may use the shortcut:
L.
Where marks actually go
Celsius left in a ratio. Costs the whole question, every time.
An unbalanced equation. The mole ratio comes from the coefficients, so a wrong balance makes every later step wrong while looking perfectly tidy.
Using 22.4 L/mol away from STP.
R mismatched to the units — kPa with the atm value of R.
Ratios flipped. A gas that was heated must expand. Check the direction against common sense before writing the answer down.
Getting help with Chemistry 11

Gas laws are one of the few Chemistry 11 topics where the concept is easier than the bookkeeping — most students who struggle here understand the physics fine and are losing marks to units, conversions and ratio direction. That is very fixable, and quickly. Our
one-on-one Chemistry 11 help
starts by finding out which of the two it actually is.
Everything here reappears in
Chemistry 12
under equilibrium and kinetics, where partial pressures assume you already own PV = nRT. Sessions run in person in Burnaby or online across Metro Vancouver, aligned to the BC curriculum.
Book a free 30-minute consultation
and bring a recent test.

children.text: Calculus has a reputation for being the hard one, and it is the wrong reputation. The mechanics of differentiating are easier than most of Pre-Calculus 12 — the power rule takes about a minute to learn.

What is genuinely hard is the first idea: the limit. Everything in the course is built on it, most students never quite get it, and they compensate by memorising rules. That works for a term, right up until a question asks what a derivative means rather than what it equals.
This guide does the idea first and the rules second, which is the order that makes them stick. If you would rather work through it with someone, our
Calculus 12 tutoring
starts in exactly this place.
A limit is about approaching, not arriving
Here is the question that unlocks the course. Consider:
Substitute
and you get
— undefined. The function does not exist at
. And yet the limit exists, and equals 4.
The cancellation is legal for one reason worth stating precisely:
means
gets arbitrarily close to 2
without ever equalling it
. So
, and dividing by it is allowed.

Sit with what that says. The function has a hole at x = 2 — it genuinely has no value there. But everywhere nearby it behaves exactly like x + 2, so as you close in on 2 from either side, the outputs close in on 4. A limit describes where a function is heading, not where it arrives, and those are different questions.

Students who never separate those two questions find continuity mysterious, then the derivative impossible — because the derivative is a limit at a point where substitution gives 0/0, every single time.
The derivative is one picture
Forget the formula for a moment. The problem the derivative solves is this: how steep is a curve at a single point?

That question is awkward. Slope needs two points — rise over run. One point gives you nothing to divide. So we cheat: take a second point nearby, find the slope of the line through both (a secant), then slide the second point closer and closer and watch what the slope does.
The dashed lines are secants through P(3, 9). Watch their slopes as the second point approaches P:
— second point (4, 16), slope
— slope
— slope
— slope
The slopes are not wandering. They are settling on 6 — and 6 is the slope of the tangent at P. That settling is the derivative, and the limit is the machinery that makes "settling" precise:
Read it as the picture, not as symbols:
is the rise,
is the run, and
is the second point sliding into the first.

And notice why this needs a limit at all: at h = 0 exactly, the fraction is 0/0. The one value you actually want is the one value you cannot substitute. That is not a technicality — it is the reason limits exist.
Worked example: the derivative from first principles
Find
for
using the definition.
Expand the top
Divide — and here is why it works
That cancellation is only legal because
— we are approaching zero, not sitting on it. It is the same move as the first example, and it is the move the whole technique depends on.
Now take the limit
At
— exactly the number the secants were settling on. The picture and the algebra agree, which is the point of doing it once by hand.

You will use the power rule from here on and never do this again. Do it once anyway. The rule is a shortcut for this process, and a student who has seen the process knows what the shortcut is short for.
The tangent line, and what the question is really asking
"Find the equation of the tangent to
at
" is two questions wearing one coat.
A slope question — which is calculus, and takes one line
A straight-line question — which is Grade 9, and is where the marks are lost
Check it: at
. ✓ The line touches the curve at P, as it must.
The classic error is giving 6 as the answer. The question asked for an equation; 6 is a slope. Read what was asked.
The rules, and what each is for
Once the idea is in place, the rules are quick — but knowing which to reach for is the skill:
The chain rule decides your grade
More marks turn on the chain rule than on anything else, because it hides inside every other rule.
Say it as you write: derivative of the outside, leaving the inside alone, times the derivative of the inside. The universal failure is stopping halfway — writing cos(x²) and forgetting the 2x.
Rules inside rules

The product rule ran, the chain rule ran inside its second term, and then — the step students skip — the answer was factored. On an exam an unsimplified answer costs marks and makes the next part harder than it needs to be.
What a derivative means when it isn't a graph
The tangent picture is how the derivative is taught, and it quietly limits students — because exam questions rarely mention tangents. They ask about rates.
A derivative is a rate of change: how fast one quantity changes as another does. The tangent slope is that idea drawn for the special case where the two quantities are
and
. Change the letters and the same derivative answers a different question.
If
is position at time
, then
is velocity — how fast position changes
Differentiate again and
is acceleration — how fast velocity changes
If
is the cost of making
items,
is the cost of making one more
If
is the volume of a balloon,
is how fast it is inflating

This is why calculus escaped mathematics and took over physics, economics and engineering. It is not a technique for finding tangents — it is the mathematics of things changing, and the tangent is simply the easiest instance to draw.

It also explains a question type that ambushes students: "what does f'(3) = 6 mean in this context?" There is no algebra to do. The answer is a sentence — at x = 3, the quantity is increasing at 6 units per unit of x — and students who only ever saw slopes have nothing to write.
Notation, and why there are two of them
Two notations appear for the same thing, and nobody explains why:
They mean the same derivative.
is compact and reads well when you are differentiating a named function.
keeps both variables visible, which matters the moment there are more than two things changing.
That second form earns its keep in related rates, where you will write
and
in the same line and need to see at a glance what is changing with respect to what. It is worth being fluent in both now, because the course switches between them without warning.
Read

as "the rate at which y changes as x changes" rather than as a fraction. It is not a fraction — though it behaves enough like one that the chain rule looks like cancelling, which is a useful coincidence and a dangerous habit.
Where marks actually go
Treating a limit as "substitute and see" — it works until 0/0, which is exactly when it matters
Stopping the chain rule halfway:
instead of
Answering a tangent-line question with a slope
Leaving the answer unsimplified, then fighting it in part (b)
Memorising the rules without once doing a derivative from the definition — so when a question asks what f'(3) means, there is nothing to say
Practice problems
1. Differentiate
2. Evaluate
3. Find the equation of the tangent to
at
Solutions
1. Chain rule
Outside is
, inside is
The 6x is the whole question. Leave it out and you have written the outside derivative and stopped.
2. Factor, then cancel
Same shape as the opening example:
on substitution, a factor that cancels because
, and a limit that exists even though the function does not.
3. Slope, point, line
Check: at
. ✓ The negative slope is worth a glance — the parabola is falling at
, so it should be.
Why this matters beyond the grade

Calculus 12 is the prerequisite for first-year calculus at UBC and SFU, and those courses do not revisit it — they assume it and move faster. Every idea above reappears there within weeks, and the students who struggle are almost never struggling with calculus: they are struggling with the algebra underneath it, at speed. We wrote about that in
what UBC calculus students should review before their first midterm
It also runs straight back into
Pre-Calculus 12
— factoring, trig identities and function notation are the tools every derivative question is actually testing.
Getting help with Calculus 12
If the rules make sense but the questions do not, the gap is usually the first idea rather than the mechanics — and that is a fast thing to fix in person and a slow thing to fix from a textbook. Our
one-on-one Calculus 12 help
starts by finding out which of the two it is.

children.text: Physics 12 is not a maths problem. That is the single most useful thing to know about it, and almost nobody says it out loud.

Students arrive able to rearrange equations perfectly well, and they still lose marks — because the question is a paragraph about a toboggan, and the marks are for turning that paragraph into a diagram. Once the diagram is right, the algebra is Grade 10 work. Once the diagram is wrong, no amount of algebra saves it.
So this guide spends its time where the marks are. If you would rather work through it with someone, our
Physics 12 tutoring
starts in exactly this place — with the picture, not the formula sheet.
Kinematics describes. Dynamics explains.
The course splits in two, and the split is worth naming because students blur it constantly.
Kinematics describes motion — where, how fast, how quickly that speed changes. It never asks why. A kinematics question can be answered without knowing whether the object is a car, a comet or a cat.
Dynamics explains motion — it brings in forces and mass, and answers why the acceleration has the value it has.

They meet at one quantity: acceleration. Dynamics works out what the acceleration is, using forces. Kinematics takes that acceleration and works out what happens over time. When a long problem seems to have two unrelated halves, that is what it is doing — find the acceleration with Newton, then feed it into kinematics.
The five equations, and how to actually choose one
There are five kinematics equations for constant acceleration. Between them they involve five quantities:
(initial velocity),
(final velocity),
(acceleration),
(displacement) and
(time).
Each equation is missing exactly one of the five. That is not a coincidence — it is the whole selection method.

So the method is: list what you have, list what you want, and find the quantity you neither have nor want. Take the equation that is missing it. This turns equation choice from a guess into a lookup, and it is worth practising until it is automatic.
Worked example
A car braking from 25 m/s comes to rest in 40 m. Find the acceleration.
We have
. We want
. We neither have nor want
— so use the equation with no
in it.

The minus sign is not decoration. It says the acceleration points opposite to the motion, which is what braking means. A student who writes 7.8 has not made a small error — they have described a car speeding up.
And if the question then wants the time, kinematics hands it over:
gives
s.
Signs are a decision, not a fact
Half of all lost kinematics marks are sign errors, and they come from treating direction as something the universe decides. It isn't. You decide.

Pick a positive direction at the start, write it down at the top of your work, and then commit to it for the entire question. Everything pointing that way is positive, everything pointing the other way is negative, and that includes gravity.
If you call up positive, then

m/s². Not sometimes. Always, for that question. The most common disaster is a student who calls up positive at the start, then silently flips to down-positive halfway through because the object started falling. The object does not care which way you called positive. The equations do.
The free-body diagram is the actual work

Here is where dynamics is won or lost. A free-body diagram strips away the ramp, the rope, the toboggan and the snow, and leaves one object and the arrows pushing on it. Draw it correctly and the question is nearly finished.
Three rules make free-body diagrams reliable:
Only forces ON the object, never forces the object exerts on something else. This kills the phantom "forward force" students draw on a moving car.
Only real forces. If you cannot name the thing touching the object — or say the word gravity — it is not a force. There is no such thing as a leftover "force of motion".
Choose axes along the motion. On an incline, tilt the axes to match the slope. Nothing forces you to use horizontal and vertical, and on a ramp those axes make the work three times harder.
The normal force is not mg
This is the misconception that costs the most marks in the course, because it is right often enough to feel like a rule.
On a flat floor with nothing pressing down, yes:

. But the normal force is not a formula — it is the surface pushing back just hard enough to stop the object sinking into it. Tilt the surface and it pushes back less, because part of the weight is now sliding the object along rather than into the ramp.
Take the block in the diagram:
kg on a 30° slope. Its weight is
N. But perpendicular to the slope:
Not 39.2 N. And this matters immediately, because friction is calculated from N — so an incorrect normal force poisons every line after it.
Resolving the weight
The dashed arrows in the diagram are the move that makes inclines work. The weight points straight down, which is along neither axis, so it gets rewritten as two pieces:
Down the slope:
N — this is what accelerates the block.
Into the slope:
N — this is what the normal force balances.

Those two pieces are not extra forces. They are the same weight, written in a more convenient pair of directions, and they recombine to exactly 39.2 N. Adding mg AND its components to the same diagram is double-counting, and it is a common way to lose a mark for free.
Applying Newton's second law along the slope, with no friction:
Notice the mass cancels. A heavy block and a light block slide down a frictionless ramp identically — which is Galileo's result, hiding in one line of algebra.
Now add friction
With a coefficient of kinetic friction
, friction opposes the sliding, so it acts up the slope:
Slower than 4.9 m/s², as it must be. And this form quietly answers a favourite exam question — when does the block not slide at all? When the friction available exceeds
, which happens when
. At 30°, that is
. The angle alone decides it; the mass is irrelevant.
Newton's laws, minus the slogans
Everyone can recite them. Fewer can say what they claim.

First law — objects keep doing what they are doing unless a net force acts. The real content is that motion needs no cause. Only a change in motion does. This is the opposite of everyday intuition, which is why it took humanity two thousand years.
Second law —
. The word that carries the weight is net. It is never one force; it is the sum of every arrow on the diagram. If your answer is wrong, the sum is where to look first.

Third law — forces come in equal and opposite pairs. The catch: the two forces act on different objects, so they never cancel. If they did, nothing could ever accelerate. The horse still pulls the cart.
Projectiles are two stories at once
Projectile motion looks like new material and is not. It is the kinematics you already have, run twice — because the horizontal and vertical motions are completely independent and share only a clock.
Horizontally there is no force (ignoring air), so
and the horizontal velocity never changes. Vertically,
m/s² the whole time — on the way up, at the top, on the way down.
Throw a ball at 20 m/s at 35°. Split it once at the start:
The time in the air comes from the vertical story alone:
s. The range comes from the horizontal story alone:
m. Maximum height, again vertical only:
m.

The idea worth carrying: at the very top of the arc the ball is not stopped. Its vertical velocity is zero, but it is still moving sideways at 16.4 m/s, and it is still accelerating downwards at 9.8 m/s². "Velocity is zero" and "acceleration is zero" are unrelated statements, and an exam will check that you know it.
Three to try
1. Pushing a box
A 12 kg box is pushed across level ground with a horizontal 60 N force.
. Find the acceleration.
Here the push is horizontal, so nothing changes the vertical balance:
N. Then
N, and:

Worth noticing why N = mg was legal here but not on the ramp: the surface is flat and the push has no vertical component. Push downwards at an angle instead and N grows, friction grows with it, and the box gets harder to move — which is exactly why you pull a sled rather than push it.
2. The elevator
You stand on a bathroom scale in a lift, mass 60 kg, accelerating upward at 2.0 m/s². What does the scale read?
The scale reads the normal force, not your weight — that is what a scale physically measures.

body.latex: N - mg = ma \quad \Longrightarrow \quad N = m(g + a) = 60(11.8) = 708 \ \text{N}

children.text: Against

N standing still. Your mass has not changed by a gram; the surface is simply pushing harder. Accelerate downward at 2.0 m/s² instead and it reads 468 N — the lurch in your stomach as a lift sets off, quantified.
3. Sign discipline
A ball is thrown straight up at 15 m/s from a 2.0 m height. Taking up as positive, write down the values of v₀, a, and Δx when it lands — before solving anything.
(still negative on the way up), and
— because it finishes 2.0 m below where it started. Most students who get this question wrong get the sign of
wrong, not the physics.
Where marks actually go
From marking a lot of these papers, the pattern barely changes:
No free-body diagram, or one drawn after the algebra as decoration. The diagram is worth marks on its own and it prevents the errors below.
Using mg where mg cos θ belongs, then propagating it through friction into every subsequent line.
Sign flips mid-question.
Skipping units, or mixing cm with m. Physics 12 gives marks for units and takes them away for missing ones.
Never asking whether the answer is sensible. A toboggan at 340 m/s is a mistake, not an answer, and a two-second sanity check catches it.
The maths underneath

When a student struggles in Physics 12, it is genuinely often not physics. It is trigonometry — resolving vectors is nothing but sine and cosine — or it is rearranging an equation with three symbols in it. That is why

children.text: "He understands it when we go through it, but then he gets them wrong on the test." Almost every parent who contacts a tutor says some version of this, and it is the single most useful sentence to unpack — because it describes two completely different problems that need opposite treatments.

Get the diagnosis wrong and months disappear. A student with a concept gap given more practice questions simply practises the misunderstanding until it is permanent. A student with a practice gap given more explanation sits through lessons they already understand, gets bored, and still runs out of time in the exam.
The distinction is not subtle once you know what to look for, and you can test it at the kitchen table in about ten minutes.
The two failure modes
A concept gap

The student does not understand what the mathematics means. They may still get answers right — by mimicking a worked example closely enough — which is exactly what makes this hard to spot from a report card.
It looks like:
They can do a question that matches an example, but stall completely when the wording changes
They cannot say why a step is done, only that it comes next
Wrong answers are wrong in strange ways — not close, but structurally off
They ask "what do I do here?" rather than "did I do this right?"
Progress collapses whenever a topic builds on the shaky one
A practice gap
The student understands the material. The knowledge is simply not fast or automatic enough to survive a timed test.
It looks like:
They can explain the method correctly, out loud, without notes
Mistakes are arithmetic slips, dropped signs, copying errors — "silly mistakes"
They run out of time, or rush the last questions
Homework is fine; tests are not
Shown the mistake, they immediately see it — no explanation needed
The ten-minute test
Here is the diagnostic, and it works because it separates knowing from doing.
Take a question they got wrong. Do not ask them to solve it. Ask them to explain how they would solve it — out loud, without writing anything and without touching the numbers.
If they can talk you through the method confidently and only fall apart when executing it — that is a practice gap.
If the explanation is vague, circular, or reaches for the textbook — that is a concept gap, regardless of what their homework marks look like.

The reason this works: explaining requires understanding, while doing can be faked by pattern-matching. Most school assessment rewards doing, so a concept gap can stay hidden for a long time — often until the course builds on it and everything appears to collapse at once.

A second, blunter version: ask "why does that step work?" A practice-gap student answers, sometimes impatiently. A concept-gap student explains what the step is again, more slowly. Watch for that substitution — it is the tell.
Why they need opposite treatments
A concept gap needs rebuilding, not repetition

More questions will not help, and can actively harm. Every repetition of a misunderstood method makes it more automatic and harder to dislodge. The fix is to go back — often further back than feels reasonable — find the idea that never landed, and rebuild from there.

This feels like losing ground. Parents often resist it, because the student is behind and going backwards seems like the opposite of catching up. But a concept gap is load-bearing: everything stacked on it is unstable, and time spent stacking higher is time wasted.
A practice gap needs volume and timing

Explanation is not the constraint — the student already understands. What they need is enough repetition that the method becomes automatic, and enough timed practice that exam conditions stop being a separate skill.

Re-teaching a practice-gap student is a common and expensive mistake. They already know it. What they cannot yet do is retrieve it in ninety seconds with a clock running, and no amount of further explanation builds that.
The trap: "silly mistakes"
This phrase hides both problems, which is why it is worth interrogating.
Sometimes a silly mistake really is one: a dropped minus sign, a misread digit. That is a practice gap, and repetition fixes it.

But often "silly mistake" is what a student calls an error they cannot explain. If they consistently make the same silly mistake in the same place, it is not carelessness — it is a misunderstanding wearing a friendlier name. The test is whether they can tell you why it was wrong. If they can only tell you that it was wrong, look closer.
Both at once

The honest complication: it is often both. A concept gap in one topic, and a practice gap everywhere else. The order matters — fix the concept first, then build the speed, because drilling an idea that is not yet understood cements the wrong version.

It also changes over a term. A student who started with a concept gap and has had it repaired will look, for a few weeks, exactly like a student with a practice gap — because that is now what they are. The diagnosis is not permanent, and it is worth re-running.
What this means for choosing help
It is worth knowing which problem you are buying help for, because they look identical from the outside and cost the same.
A homework club or worksheet service is practice. Useful for a practice gap; nearly useless for a concept gap
A group class re-explains the curriculum. Useful if the explanation is the constraint; not if the student needs volume
One-on-one tutoring can do either — but only if the tutor diagnoses first rather than starting from page one
This is the reason our
free 30-minute consultation
is a conversation rather than a lesson: the diagnosis genuinely determines what we would do, and getting it wrong wastes your money as well as your child's term.
What to do this week
Take one wrong answer from a recent test — not a homework question.
Ask them to explain the method out loud, without writing or touching the numbers.
Listen for whether they explain WHY, or only re-describe WHAT.
If they can explain it: practice gap. Give them volume and a timer.
If they cannot: concept gap. Stop the practice, go back, and rebuild.

That is a real diagnosis, and it costs ten minutes. It is worth considerably more than another purchased workbook — because the workbook is only the right treatment for one of the two problems, and you now know which.
If you would like a second opinion
We do this diagnosis at the start of every relationship, because starting to teach before you know which problem you are solving is guesswork. Our
one-on-one math tutoring in Burnaby
and science support work the same way, whether the answer turns out to be a concept gap, a practice gap, or the usual mix of both.
Sessions run in person in Burnaby or online across Metro Vancouver.
Book a free 30-minute consultation
— we will work through a recent test together and tell you honestly which of the two you are dealing with, even if the answer is that no tutoring is needed yet.

children.text: Straight answer first, because that is what you came for.
One-on-one tutoring: $75–$100 per hour, depending on subject and level.
Monthly Program: $185–$200 per month — two sessions a week, in a small group of six to eight.
Exam Booster: $280 for a two-week intensive course.

No registration fee, no assessment fee, no materials fee, no contract, and the first conversation costs nothing. That is the whole price list. The rest of this article is about which of those three is right for your child, and — genuinely — when none of them are.
Why one-on-one is a range instead of a number
The $75–$100 spread is about the level of the work, not about how much we think you will pay.

Grade 8 math and second-year university calculus take a different amount of preparation, and the preparation is most of the job. An hour of Pre-Calculus 11 might need fifteen minutes of setup. An hour of university linear algebra, taught against a specific professor's notation and a specific midterm, can need an hour of setup before the session starts. You are told which end of the range applies before you book, not after.
What does not change the price: how urgently you need it, how worried you sound on the phone, or whether it is exam season.
What a session actually costs to deliver
It is worth knowing what the hourly rate is paying for, because "an hour of tutoring" is not an hour of work.
The hour itself.
Preparation before it — reading the actual test your child failed, not a generic worksheet.
The diagnosis. Working out whether the problem is the topic on the page or something from two years earlier.
A qualified person. These sessions are taught by someone with a PhD in ultrasound and signal processing, who used this mathematics professionally rather than only studying it.

That last point is the one parents most often underrate, and it cuts both ways. For Grade 8 arithmetic, a PhD is genuinely overkill and you should not pay for one. For Calculus 12, Physics 12, or a first-year university course going badly, the difference between a tutor who knows the answer and one who knows why the student cannot see it is the entire value of the hour.
The comparison nobody does for you
Per session, the two main options look very different:
The Monthly Program is $185–$200 for two sessions a week. Two a week is about
sessions a month, so:
Roughly a quarter of the one-on-one rate. So why would anyone pay four times as much?
Because they are not the same product, and the honest answer is that they do different jobs:

The Monthly Program is for consistent practice, accountability and momentum across a term. It works when your child broadly understands the material and needs reps, structure, and someone noticing when they drift.

One-on-one is for diagnosis and repair. It works when something specific is broken and nobody has found it yet. In a group of seven, that hunt cannot happen — the tutor's attention is divided seven ways, which is exactly why the group rate is a quarter of the price.
If you know what is wrong, the group is better value. If you do not know what is wrong, the group will not find out, and the cheaper rate is a false economy.
The number that actually matters is not the hourly rate
Here is where most families lose money, and it has nothing to do with choosing an expensive tutor over a cheap one.
It is buying tutoring that never ends. Compare two ways of spending at the same $85 an hour:
Supervised homework. A tutor sits with your child weekly, helps with tonight's assignment, and the marks stay flat because nobody ever asked why. Two terms of that is 20 sessions:
Targeted repair. Session one finds the actual gap — usually something from an earlier year. Six sessions fix it, and the tutoring stops:

Same tutor. Same hourly rate. A difference of $1,190 — and the cheaper one is also the one that worked. The expensive option is not the higher rate; it is the arrangement with no diagnosis and no end date.
So the question worth asking a tutor is not "what do you charge?" It is "how will you know when we are done?" A tutor who cannot answer that is selling you the $1,700 version.
Working out which kind of problem you have is something you can partly do at the kitchen table before spending anything. We wrote a guide to telling a
concept gap from a practice gap
, and it is the single most useful twenty minutes a parent can spend on this.
When tutoring is not worth your money
Not many tutoring websites have this section. It matters more than the price list.

The problem is not mathematics. If your child is anxious, sleeping badly, or something changed at school or at home, tutoring treats a symptom and the real thing gets worse while you pay for it. Address that first — we will say so on the call.
Homework is getting done and marks are fine. Some students are simply finding it hard because it is hard. That is not a gap; that is learning.
Nobody has talked to the teacher yet. It is free, they have information nobody else has, and it sometimes ends the problem outright.
The student has flatly refused. Tutoring works on a student who is fed up and willing. It does not work on one who has been sent as a punishment, and we would rather tell you than take the booking.
We have turned down work on all four of these. It costs us a booking and saves you several hundred dollars, and we would rather have the reputation.
Five questions worth asking any tutor
These work on us and they work on anyone else you are considering. If you only take one thing from this page, take these.
1. How will you know when we are done?
The single most revealing question you can ask. A tutor with a plan can describe an end state. A tutor without one will talk about ongoing support, which is a business model rather than an answer.
2. What will you do in the first session?

You want to hear diagnosis — looking at past tests, finding where the working breaks down, checking assumed knowledge from earlier years. If the answer is "start the current unit", they are treating the symptom on the page.
3. Who is actually teaching my child?

At larger centres the person you speak to is often not the person who teaches, and the teacher may be a strong student a few years older. That can be perfectly fine for early high school. It is not fine for Calculus 12. Ask, and ask what happens if that person leaves mid-term.
4. What am I paying for outside the session?
Registration fees, assessment fees, materials, minimum terms, cancellation rules. All legitimate, all worth knowing before rather than after. Ask for the number you will actually pay in month one.
5. When would you tell me not to bother?
If a tutor cannot think of a single situation where their service is the wrong answer, either they have not thought about it or they are not going to tell you. Both should give you pause.
Does online cost less?
No — the rate is the same, and it is worth saying why, because plenty of places do charge less for online and it is reasonable to wonder.

The preparation, the diagnosis and the qualification of the person teaching do not change with the medium. The only thing that changes is the room. For most of high school and essentially all university work, a shared screen with proper equation software is as good as sitting side by side, and for some things it is better — the whole session can be saved and re-read afterwards, which a whiteboard cannot do.

Where in person genuinely wins is younger students, anyone who fidgets their way out of a video call, and the specific moment when a student needs someone to watch their hand while they write and catch the error as it happens. If that is your child, come to Burnaby. If it is not, online saves you the drive and costs you nothing in quality.
What the free consultation actually is
Thirty minutes, no charge, no obligation, and it is not a sales call — there is nothing to sign at the end of it.

Bring a recent test, ideally one that went badly. That single piece of paper carries more information than an hour of description: which questions were left blank, where the working stops, whether the errors are conceptual or arithmetic. Most of a diagnosis is visible in it.

By the end you should have three things: an honest read on what is actually wrong, a rough idea of how many sessions it should take, and a clear answer on whether it is worth doing at all. If the answer is no, you will hear that, and it costs you nothing but the half hour.
Then, if it makes sense, sessions run in person in Burnaby — parking is free — or online across Metro Vancouver, between 9am and 8pm.
The honest bit about value
Nobody can promise you a grade. Any tutor who does is guessing, and any tutor who quotes you an average improvement is quoting a number they cannot support.

What can be said honestly is this. Pre-Calculus 12 is a prerequisite. If it does not get fixed, the cost is not a lower mark — it is a repeated course, a delayed application, or a program that quietly stops being available. Set against that, six sessions is a small number, and the reason to act early is that gaps compound: every month a foundation stays broken, more of the new material gets built on top of it, and the repair gets longer.
That is the actual argument for tutoring, and it does not require any exaggeration.

, bring a recent test, and we will tell you honestly whether this is worth your money.
